_verification: Every entry below was cross-checked against AT LEAST the sources named. Where the sources spell the same phrase differently (dhanyabad / dhanyabaad / dhanyabād), the form used here is the one the majority of sources use, and the variation is noted rather than hidden.
_NOT_VERIFIED_BY_A_NATIVE_SPEAKER: This is the honest limit. I am not a Nepali speaker and no native speaker has checked this file. Nepali has a prestige register (tapai/hajur) and a familiar one (timi/ta) — getting that wrong is not a grammar error, it is a social one. Treat every phrase as PROVISIONAL until a colleague confirms it. The engine's job is to make the mistake cheap and the correction easy; the colleague's job is to be right.
label: Nepali — Central (ne-NP)

register._note: Nepali marks respect INSIDE the verb and pronoun, not with a particle like Thai's khrap/kha. So there is no 'male form' / 'female form' here — the split that exists in Thai does not exist in Nepali, and inventing one would be a lie about the language.
register.familiar: timi / ta — for close friends and children only, NEVER for a colleague you have just met

greeting.note: Universal. Palms together. Use any time of day — it is not time-of-day specific like Thai's sawatdee.
Added 2026-10-26 from the UBC textbook's Ch.2 list — the register step up from namaste.
The standard polite form — for a colleague, a shopkeeper, anyone you are not close to.
The answer to the line above.
Added 2026-10-26 (Jordan asked for 'how about you'). 'ani' = and. ASK IT — a greeting that does not bounce back is not a conversation.
Casual — fine with a colleague you have spoken to before; skip it on day one.
Sources also write ‘dhanyabaad’ / ‘dhanyabād’. Same word, different romanisation.
‘dherai’ = much/very. Use it when someone actually helped you.
For an apology. Also works to get past someone in a crowd.
The all-purpose 'sounds good' — you will hear it a hundred times a shift.
The natural way to leave a conversation.

workplace.note: The single most useful phrase on a shift with colleagues whose language you are only starting.
Asking someone to slow down is polite here — it is not an admission you are failing, and saying it EARLY beats guessing.
Added 2026-10-26. Pattern: [name] ho = 'is [name]'. Swap the name and you can introduce anyone.
Point at the thing. Fastest vocabulary you will build.

people.note: Not literal family. Colleagues use these as respectful address; getting them right earns more goodwill than perfect grammar.

_register_warning_for_the_engine: Nepali has NO gendered politeness particle. Do not apply the Thai form-swap (ครับ/ค่ะ) to this dialect — a female learner saying 'dhanyabad kha' would be nonsense. All learners get the same form, and the pack declares no by_form voices.
